courseTitle: Physics 2: Fluids, Heat, Electricity, Light and Atoms
title: Electric Current
short: I = ΔQ/Δt, and conventional current points the way positive charge would flow.
trouble: Students think current gets used up as it passes through a bulb.

blocks.html: In Current and Voltage you met current as the flow of charge around a circuit. Now we measure it. Because charge is conserved, counting the charge that passes a point tells you a great deal about the whole circuit.

Stand at one point in a wire and count the charge going past. The current is how much passes per second. In a metal the moving charges are electrons, and they drift slowly, typically well under a millimeter per second, but the push that moves them spreads through the circuit almost at once, so a lamp lights the instant the switch closes. Charge cannot pile up anywhere in a steady circuit, so on a single path the same current passes every point, before and after each part.

$$\role{current}{I} = \frac{\role[charge passing]{charge}{\Delta Q}}{\role[time interval]{time}{\Delta t}}, \qquad 1\,\text{A} = 1\,\text{C/s}$$ Conventional current points the way positive charge would flow: out of the battery's $+$ terminal, around the circuit, and back into its $-$ terminal. In wires, electrons drift the opposite way.

opts.task: The moving dots are the current. Count them going into the bulb and coming out.

blocks.title: Finding a current
blocks.q: $3.0\,\text{C}$ of charge passes a point in $1.5\,\text{s}$. What is the current?

blocks.title: Charge and electrons
blocks.q: A current of $0.50\,\text{A}$ flows for $2.0$ minutes. How much charge passes, and how many electrons is that?

blocks.html: Thinking current gets used up as it passes through a bulb, so less comes out than goes in. The charge that goes in must come out; otherwise it would pile up inside the bulb. What the bulb uses is energy: each coulomb leaves at a lower potential than it entered. Check: put an ammeter on each side of the bulb; both read the same.
